text: New York, the Independent Rent Guidelines Board just froze the rent. That means if you're one of the more than 2 million New Yorkers who lives in a rent-stabilized apartment, your rent's going to be frozen next year. Many of you wanted me to specifically break down the NYC housing situation and Mamdani's rent freeze. So let's do that. I want to start with the core idea. Mamdani's rent freeze is not a magical button that freezes all rents in New York City. It doesn't apply to every apartment. It doesn't apply to normal market-rate apartments. It applies to rent-stabilized apartments, roughly 1 million apartments in the city. That is about 41% of all rental units in NYC. And the idea is simple. If you already live in a rent-stabilized apartment, your landlord cannot raise your rent for the covered renewal period. The Rent Guidelines Board approved a 0% increase for 1-year and 2-year leases. So for those tenants, yes, this is real relief. But again, only for people already inside that system. Now, what are rent-stabilized apartments? They are not public housing. Public housing is something like NYCHA, where the government is directly involved and tenants are usually lower income. Rent-stabilized apartments are usually privately-owned apartments, but the government limits how much the rent can go up. Tenants also have stronger renewal rights. In general, rent stabilization applies to older buildings built before 1974, with 6 or more apartments. There are also newer buildings that became rent-stabilized because the owner received tax benefits or participated in affordable housing programs. And this is important. This is not some tiny side program. Rate stabilization has shaped New York housing for decades. In 2023, about 76% of rent-stabilized units were there through the old Emergency Tenant Protection Act route. Basically, the older, legacy rent-stabilized stock. So when we talk about Mamdani's rent freeze, we're talking about adding a freeze on top of a system that has already affected NYC housing for half a century. And in 2019, the rules became much stricter. Before that, some apartments could eventually leave rent stabilization through vacancy or high-rent regulation. But the 2019 reforms limited the circumstances under which apartments can exit the system. So the system became more permanent, more locked in, and less flexible. Now, why does this matter? Because NYC's housing situation is already insane. The citywide rental vacancy rate in the 2023 Housing and Vacancy Survey was only around 1.4%. The lowest since 1968. And for cheaper apartments, the situation was even worse. For apartments renting under $2,400, the vacancy rate was below 1%. In simple language, New York doesn't have enough apartments. And when a city doesn't have enough apartments, everything becomes weird. Market rate rents go up. People stay in apartments that no longer fit their lives. Young people cannot move out. Family cannot find bigger places. Newcomers cannot find anything affordable. And a lot of people end up in informal or straight-up illegal housing arrangements. I know this personally. When I lived in New York, I lived for 3 months in an illegal hostel, where 8 people were living in one room, and each person paid $500 a month. I also lived in another apartment, where I was basically just given a bed in a room to cut expenses. And this is not just my personal anecdote. NYC has official data showing crowded households, and the city receives thousands of illegal conversion complaints. So there is clearly a hidden housing market where people rent beds, split rooms, unofficially sublet, or live in spaces that were never meant to be apartments. Now, did rent stabilization alone create this mess? No, that would be too simple. New York also has zoning restrictions, slow permitting, expensive construction, neighborhood opposition, high taxes, old buildings, and decades of not building enough housing where people actually want to live. It protects people who already rent apartments, but it doesn't create new ones. It helps insiders, but it doesn't solve the problem for outsiders. So the key point is this. Mamdani's rent freeze is a real relief for some people, but it is relief for people already inside the protected part of the housing market. It doesn't freeze market rents, it doesn't create new apartments, and it doesn't solve the underlying shortage. And that brings us to the real question. Will this actually fix anything? We talk about it in the next video.
